pr_body:
This adds the `[RegexGenerator(...)]` attribute and a new System.Text.RegularExpressions.Generator source generator for Regex.  Given a method like:
```C#
[RegexGenerator("abc")]
private static partial Regex Abc();
```
it will generate C# code to implement `Abc()` that returns a `Regex` instance with code like you'd have gotten with `RegexOptions.Compiled`, but generated at build time in C# rather than at run time with reflection emit in MSIL.  The generator is largely a port of RegexCompiler.cs; ideally we wouldn't duplicate all of the emit logic, once for MSIL and once for C#, and we should subsequently look for ways to avoid this duplication.  The generator includes source from System.Text.RegularExpressions, in particular in support of parsing and analyzing regexes.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2642209/133515550-1d1bc397-192c-41c3-83c0-eb7479aae400.png)

It includes a test project for the generator focused on testing the mechanics of the generator as well as integrating the source generator into the regex test suite, rolled out into many but not all of the tests so far.

There are a bunch of follow-ups to this for while I'll be opening issues, including rolling this out through the rest of the tests (and finding ways to make it go faster, as it's currently significantly increasing the time for the regex test suite), fixing a bunch of TODOs (e.g. figuring out what to do about culture), and improving perf further (it's now really easy to see opportunities for improved code generation).

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/58880
Contributes to https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/44676

cc: @danmoseley, @pgovind, @tannergooding, @eerhardt, @veanes, @olsaarik

Note regarding the `new-api-needs-documentation` label:

This serves as a reminder for when your PR is modifying a ref *.cs file and adding/modifying public APIs, to please make sure the API implementation in the src *.cs file is documented with triple slash comments, so the PR reviewers can sign off that change.
Will actually be interesting now we can look at the C# generated for different regexes to more easily see how it works.
Will there be any warning if that library code (supposed to be language agnostic?) would be called NOT from Roslyn?

> Will there be any warning if that library code (supposed to be language agnostic?) would be called NOT from Roslyn?

I don't understand the question.  `Regex` is usable from all .NET languages.  If you try to use `RegexGenerator` with something other than C#, you'll get errors because no code will be generated.  Can you clarify?

> > Will there be any warning if that library code (supposed to be language agnostic?) would be called NOT from Roslyn?
> 
> I don't understand the question. `Regex` is usable from all .NET languages. If you try to use `RegexGenerator` with something other than C#, you'll get errors because no code will be generated. Can you clarify?

I was worrying that somebody could try to use BCL code from F# following your example
```fsharp
type Foo() =
    [<DefaultValue; RegexGenerator("abc", RegexOptions.IgnoreCase)>]
    val mutable regex: Regex
    
let foo = Foo()
foo.regex.Match("abc")
```
and it will fail only in runtime

It would be nice to have some kind of warning if these BCL attributes are only usable from specific compiler - Roslyn.

> It would be nice to have some kind of warning if these BCL attributes are only usable from specific compiler - Roslyn.

@ericstj, where did we land on the approach of having generators inject the attribute they rely on (attributed as conditional if desired so it doesn't pollute the final assembly)? That avoids this kind of issue,  but we didn't take that approach with the other generators.  Should we reconsider moving forward?

> Regarding the Mono WASM failures

Yeah, I'd suppressed those failures for the main test project but forgot to do so for the generator test project.

If code annotates two or more identical regexes, do we unify and write out only one implementation? I'm not sure how plausible that is, but it's possible. Eg., not everyone realizes that they are thread safe.

> do we unify and write out only one implementation?

No. We could,  it's "just code", but currently I don't think it's worth the extra complexity for what should be a rare case the developer can address themselves. And I don't buy the thread-safety argument: a) the dev is writing a static method,  not a property, which they can call any number of times to get any number of instances... whether it returns the same or a new instance on each call is an implementation detail, and b) if that were really an issue,  they would likely need some way to source gen a new implementation per thread, which isn't a thing (outside of our tests).

>             writer.WriteLine($"{rm.Modifiers} Regex {rm.MethodName}() => {id}.Instance;");

With the Logging and Json generators, we fully qualify type names in the generated code. Do we want to here, as well?

ex. `global::System.Text.Json.Serialization.Metadata.JsonMetadataServices`.

---
Refers to: src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/gen/RegexGenerator.Emitter.cs:142 in 9684067. [](commit_id = 9684067d4c999e467fbc388411a0fad0d2c1ffde, deletion_comment = False)

>             writer.Write($"    public static Regex Instance {{ get; }} = ");

(nit) Could be simplified by not using `$`:

`writer.Write("    public static Regex Instance { get; } = ");`

---
Refers to: src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/gen/RegexGenerator.Emitter.cs:148 in 9684067. [](commit_id = 9684067d4c999e467fbc388411a0fad0d2c1ffde, deletion_comment = False)

> With the Logging and Json generators, we fully qualify type names in the generated code. Do we want to here, as well?

Which part are you suggesting be fully qualified?  The `{id}` part?  Is there a benefit to doing so here?

> Which part are you suggesting be fully qualified?

The references to framework types. `Regex` => `global::System.Text.RegularExpressions.Regex`.

> Is there a benefit to doing so here?

The benefit is that if the user's project/namespace declares types that conflict with our type names, the code still compiles.

See also - https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/52279

> The references to framework types

Ah, I thought you were referring to the generated types.  Sure.

issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: [RegexGenerator(...)] attribute
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @eerhardt, @dotnet/area-system-text-regularexpressions See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
### Background and motivation Attribute to trigger regex source generation: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/44676 ### API Proposal ```C# namespace System.Text.RegularExpressions { [AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Method, AllowMultiple = false, Inherited = false)] public sealed class RegexGeneratorAttribute : Attribute { // Same three constructors as on Regex, except the timeout is an int (ms) instead of a TimeSpan public RegexGeneratorAttribute(string pattern); public RegexGeneratorAttribute(string pattern, RegexOptions options); public RegexGeneratorAttribute(string pattern, RegexOptions options, int matchTimeout); public string Pattern { get; } public RegexOptions Options { get; } public int MatchTimeout { get; } } } ``` ### API Usage ```C# [RegexGenerator(@"\b[t]\w+", RegexOptions.IgnoreCase | RegexOptions.InvariantCulture)] private static partial Regex GetRegexToFindWordsBeginningWithT(); ... Regex r = GetRegexToFindWordsBeginningWithT(); foreach (Match m in r.Matches(input)) { ... } ``` ### Risks n/a
Author: stephentoub
Assignees: -
Labels: `area-System.Text.RegularExpressions`, `api-ready-for-review`
Milestone: 7.0.0
Is the instance cached or do you get a new regex every call?
It hasn't been implemented yet, so, neither :)  But my intention is that it gets cached as a singleton.

If the method were to return a cached singleton or would otherwise be cheap to call, could/should this be done via a field/property rather than a method?
e.g.
```csharp
[RegexGenerator(@"\b[t]\w+", RegexOptions.IgnoreCase | RegexOptions.InvariantCulture)]
private static readonly Regex RegexToFindWordsBeginningWithT;

// or

[RegexGenerator(@"\b[t]\w+", RegexOptions.IgnoreCase | RegexOptions.InvariantCulture)]
private static Regex RegexToFindWordsBeginningWithT { get; }
```

I'm still not very familiar with what source generators can do, but I assume they would be able to support this by outputting a static constructor to set the field/property? Although this would be a slight footgun as you could technically include this attribute for source generation, and also initialise the field yourself (which would be a silly thing to do), probably resulting in strange behaviour...

Edit: Ah, I see a class can only have a single static constructor, so my earlier idea of having a source generator output a static constructor would also preclude users from including their own static constructors, so it seems like a no-go

> could/should this be done via a field/property rather than a method?

If C# adds support for partial properties in the future,  it could support that as well.
This is a good use case for it. It also make me wonder if it would be better to support regex literals in the compiler (that's essentially what this does).

> It also make me wonder if it would be better to support regex literals in the compiler

Why?
It would feel more ergonomic and could potentially optimize more than a source generator could (it can rewrite the expression).
But one thing I'm overlooking is the regex options. I'm not sure what that would look like with literal syntax.

> it can rewrite the expression

So can the source generator. We already do optimizing / rewriting in Regex.

> one thing I'm overlooking is the regex options

And timeout.

> So can the source generator. We already do optimizing / rewriting in Regex.

It's about it feeling more natural and ergonomic. The attribute on top of a partial method doesn't feel very nice. It's working around language limitations.

> The attribute on top of a partial method doesn't feel very nice. It's working around language limitations.

Which language limitations? If you mean lack of partial properties, the source generator can easily be augmented when that's in the language. We shouldn't work around the work around by jumping straight to adding an entirely new sublanguage to C#.
Side-note: If this is done, it'd be great to have it followed-up in Roslyn by having the RegEx highlighting feature recognize this attribute.

> Which language limitations? If you mean lack of partial properties, the source generator can easily be augmented when that's in the language. We shouldn't work around the work around by jumping straight to adding an entirely new sublanguage to C#.

I was thinking of this more like a generalization of string literals. We had a similar discussion with utf8 literals, now we regex we have another potential pattern for the same thing. 

The other benefit is that you would be able to use it outside of field declarations so it could be used for locals as well.

```C#
Regex re = /^hello+/;

Console.WriteLine(re.IsMatch(args[0]));
```

@stephentoub as you pointed out offline, our current regex cache uses the actual culture name in the key (ie not just Invariant vs. Current as is in the RegexOptions). Either we have to accept that's information baked into the regex at the time it is compiled, or that's a bug we should fix. In the former case, this attribute will need to have a CultureInfo as well (the string form thereof at least)

thoughts?

> thoughts?

We need to revisit the expected behavior here around culture all-up, not just with regards to the source generator, in particular does "current culture" (when RegexOptions.CultureInvariant isn't specified) apply at construction time or at match time?  Right now, for both the interpreter and RegexOptions.Compiled, it's in a weird middle world where data from the culture that current at the time of ctor is factored in and then culture that's current at the time of match is factored in, and the implementations don't respond well to those being different.

From my perspective it's a bug that we factor it in from both.  If we choose to only factor it in at match time, the generator will match whatever we choose to do for RegexOptions.Compiled (which will likely have a perf impact).  If we choose to only factor it in from ctor time, we may want to do something special for the source generator, since (as we discussed in the API review) it's currently going to bake in the culture current at the time of build.  Options there could include just saying "yeah, you get what you get", it could include adding another ctor that takes a culture name, it could include throwing if you don't specify InvariantCulture but did specify either IgnoreCase or a pattern that employs `(?i)`, etc.

Agreed. What would be nice here is some data on what customers rely on. I'm guessing changing to "you get what you get" or "always construction time" would be breaking. We at least should be consistent if we can.

> I'm guessing changing to "you get what you get" or "always construction time" would be breaking.

Any change here is likely to break someone somewhere.  We'll need to determine what we believe is a) the "right" behavior we desire in an ideal world, b) the perf impact of that decision, and c) how widespread we expect breaks to be from that change, and make a decision.  We shouldn't do that here, though.  I'll be opening a handful of issues related to the source generator as follow-ups to address after it's initially in.

> That should already be supported via `lang=regex` comment:

Sure, but it'd be nice if this attribute is recognized so the magic comment isn't needed.

review_comments: why remove #if DEBUG?

Because the code is now used as part of the generator in release.  I could change the condition to be something like `#if DEBUG || REGEXGENERATOR`, but the linker will trim it out anyway if nothing uses it, so it didn't seem worth it.
Is it not possible to put a Regex attribute in a local method? If someone tries it, will they get a diagnostic?

It is possible, and currently there won't be a diagnostic.  With how the Initialize logic was previously structured, this wasn't possible to do well.  Now that it's set up in a way that computes diagnostics earlier in the pipeline and then passes those into Execute, I can add an analysis pass that looks through the whole tree for local functions and sees whether any have the attribute applied.  It will add additional non-trivial cost, though, which is unfortunate when it's being done purely to catch erroneous usage (and you can't write partial locals).

> (and you can't write partial locals)

ah right. Maybe we should just leave it as-is then.
Consider testing a local function as well
The methods need to be partial.  Partial locals aren't a thing.
Yeah I meant that it produces a reasonable diagnostic, not that it compiles
But it's not even valid syntax.

Thanks, but I still don't understand why a generator should have to care about that at all.  Look how many errors you get if you even try to do this:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2642209/133617248-aafafa22-2866-4a4f-b951-a758d3699071.png)

> the attribute will be added on a non-partial local function, which is a valid syntax.

You mean if the dev puts it on a non-partial local function?  I see; I can make sure the existing diagnostics fire correctly for that.

> Do we want this to be just skipped as if the attribute isn't there?

The loop you cite won't be skipping local functions, as it's iterating over members, which won't ever contain local functions.  We'd need to scour the whole syntax tree looking for local functions, in which case it seems like we'd need to essentially change IsSyntaxTargetForGeneration/GetSemanticTargetForGeneration to essentially return every method or property and then have GetRegexTypesToEmit look for any local functions that are attributed.  Is that what you're proposing be done?  Note we don't have the ability to report a diagnostic in GetSemanticTargetForGeneration, nor do I believe we have the ability to cache things like type symbols from the compilation.
Will these be documented somewhere? Might be good to attach help links (in a follow-up PR, after they're documented)
Eventually
Why `4` here and below? Doesn't just 1 indentation add 4 spaces? Is it because we are already indented 3 "manually"?

> Is it because we are already indented 3 "manually"?

Yeah.

For most of the code I rely on the indent from the writer, but here, it felt cleaner to just manually indent all the class boilerplate, to make it a bit easier to read in the generator.

Can it happen that a developer defines another version of the attribute that have `AllowMultiple = true` or different `AttributeTargets`, which can be returned by `GetTypeByMetadataName`?

I have no idea if this can happen, so just noting to consider.

> Can it happen that a developer defines another version of the attribute that have AllowMultiple = true or different AttributeTargets, which can be returned by GetTypeByMetadataName?

In theory, sure. MultipleRegexGeneratorAttributes should flag multiple.  If someone creates their own and then uses it to attribute other things, that's on them; I don't think we should be significantly increasing the cost or complexity of the generator/analyzer for such things.
is there some clever way with pattern matching to avoid all this repetition?
Suggestions welcome.
tiny nit, I find early return easier to grok generally (and less indented)..
never mind, there's value in mimicking the existing code.. at least for now.b

This is one place in the Logging Generator I'd like changed. The Json generator does it better. Instead of interpreting the parents (and potentially having bugs when new features, like file scoped namespaces, are created), I think it is better to get the TypeSymbol of the containing type, and get its namespace that way. This is how the Json generator does it.

See https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/57894#issuecomment-918247048

nit, it might be easier to read if you wrapped writer.WriteLine eg `wr(s_generatedCodeAttribute)`

in fact where there's a block of lines written together like here, perhaps it would be clearer to have one giant string so there's just one call to write.

```suggestion
        public async Task Valid_MultipleRegexMethodsPerClass()
```
As a temporary optimization, would it make sense to include all the "positive case" regex generator tests above into a single file/single test? (this one basically).. would that speed up the tests noticeably?
and maybe combine some/all of the failing ones, assuming the compiler will return all the diagnostics and we can check the line numbers match expectations.
Never mind, I see we're running the generator on far more patterns. Still I wonder whether combining might be the path to more acceptable perf.

> would that speed up the tests noticeably?

No.  These tests are very fast.  What's adding all the time is we're now running literally thousands of regexes as part of the main test suite, each of which is running the generator, compiling an assembly, etc.
a method like this is where it's fairly easy to imagine a single implementation that either emits IL or C# as requested.

Maybe, maybe not.  Even if it is, this is a tiny part of the whole implementation.

I know you care a lot about such sharing.  If you really want to move that forward, I suggest you invest a dev in prototyping it, and using this implementation as the yardstick to measure its success by.
Yup. This code certainly makes that a lot easier: it becomes essentially an exercise in how far we can reasonably reduce code duplication.
Is this because our code gen uses C# 10 features?
I think technically I ended up using only C# 9, but I've not gone back to reconfirm.
